title: Calculating Rao with R
text:
C. R. Rao lived more than 100 years and has been one of the greatest mathematicians and statisticians of the 20th century. Ecologists mostly know him for his quadratic entropy, which probably isn’t even one of his greatest achievements.
Rao’s Quadratic Entropy (Rao (2010), also called DIVC, Rao (1982)) is one of the oldest and most popular indices of functional diversity. It’s generically defined on probability distributions, but we often see what I like to call the multinomial form:
\[Q = \sum_{i}^{N}\sum_{j}^{N}d_{ij}p_{i}p_{j}\]
Call i and j two species out of N, d a distance between them, p their proportional abundances, and you have a way to calculate the average distance between two randomly drawn individuals (or more generally a weighted average distance).
While this \(\alpha\) diversity formula is well known, stopping there is also extremely reductive. Diversity partitioning across scales (something akin to \(\beta\)) has been there since the beginning, since the main goal always has been to develop a generalization of ANOVA. A unified theory tying this to other well known indices has always been there too, but today I won’t focus more on the theory, but rather on software implementations. If you want to learn more about the theory, a lot of work has been done in the last 40 years, and a lot of articles published: you can find an overview in De Benedictis et al. (2026) and its Appendix C.

title: Calculating Rao with R
text:
Setup
Just the bare minimum today.

library(conflicted)
library(tidyverse)

title: Calculating Rao with R
text:
Rao functional diversity
The example data is a snippet from the data of De Benedictis et al. (2026). This is a peculiar case, because it comes from a 1000-unit looping transect which has been resampled with overlap at several scales, so there are many sampling units, but each has few records because they come from beech forest understory. This is just one scale of one transect. For each sampling unit X, row represent observations of a species. When the sampling units are aggregates as in this case, these can be used to calculate frequencies.






Note



Want to know how we got here? Check out the twin post!



# load the preprocessed data
transect <- read_rds("transect.rds")

transect <- transect |> 
  #summarise records into species frequencies
  count(X, species) |> 
  # convert frequencies to proportions
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n), .by = X) |> 
  select(!n)

# convert data to a more traditional matrix
transect_mat <- transect |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = species, 
              values_from = prop,
              values_fill = 0) |> 
  column_to_rownames("X") |> 
  as.matrix()

title: Calculating Rao with R
text:
Custom function
As the first solution, I wanted to share a function that it’s so simple it almost feels like it shouldn’t work. The actual calculation is just one line of matrix algebra, the part before is just to get props and dist to agree. In practice, I’d always specify species, because this also ensures proportions and distances are in the same order (assuming the proportions come from a dataframe with a matching species column). Credit to this gist by Jon Lefcheck, even if the idea floats around the internet.

raoq <- function(props, dist, species = NULL){
  #subset species in the distance matrix if necessary
  if(!is.null(species)){
    dist <- dist[species, species]
  }
  
  c(crossprod(props, dist %*% props))
}

Rao sums across all species pairs the distance between i and j multiplied by the proportions of i and j to calculate an average distance. Our distance matrix already has all species pairs (optionally some that are not present, which can be subset or assigned 0 proportions), so there’s no need to loop: we just apply the matrix cross-product twice.
If you want, you could add a little check at the beginning if you want to take the species from the names of props, if present, but I prefer to be explicit with this sort of things.

if(is.null(species) && !is.null(names(props))) species <- names(props)


Matrix cross products?
To get an intuition for what the cross-product does, the first pass takes the matrix, multiplies each column by the respective value in the vector, then sums the columns together.

mat <- matrix(1:9, ncol = 3, byrow = T)
ab <- 1:3

mat

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    2    3
[2,]    4    5    6
[3,]    7    8    9

mat %*% ab

     [,1]
[1,]   14
[2,]   32
[3,]   50


The second pass takes the resulting column matrix, transposes it to a row and repeats the process (so the row of values gets summed and you end up with a single value). The c() is just so that it’s not a 1 \(\times\) 1 matrix.

c(crossprod(ab, mat %*% ab))

[1] 228

#same as
sum(mat %*% ab * ab)

[1] 228


You can double check the result with a less compact and probably slower version:

# multiply each row of mat by ab
step1 <- sweep(mat, 2, ab, "*") |> 
  # sum columns together
  rowSums()

sum(step1 * ab)

[1] 228


Back to the example. One way we can iterate raoq across multiple samples is by nesting and mapping:

transect_nested <- transect |> 
  # nest, one tibble for each X
  nest(.by = X)

# calculate Rao!
transect_nested <- transect_nested |> 
  mutate(Rao = map_dbl(data, \(x) raoq(x$prop, distances, x$species)))

title: Calculating Rao with R
text:
FD, ade4, and adiv
How would one do this with usual packages? FD::dbFD() can calculate Rao, alongside many other things which can’t all be disabled (and take time to compute).

# distance matrix must be dist and not contain extra species
dist_dbfd <- distances[colnames(transect_mat), colnames(transect_mat)] |> 
  as.dist()

rao_dbfd <- FD::dbFD(
  #first argument could be either traits or a dist object
  x = dist_dbfd,
  #abundance matrix
  a = transect_mat,
  w.abun = T,
  calc.FRic = F,
  calc.FDiv = F,
  calc.CWM = F,
  messages = F) |> 
  #just Rao, please
  pluck("RaoQ")

Under the hood, it calls ade4::divc(), which is a second option, just with a different data structure.

rao_ade4 <- ade4::divc(
  #abundances should be a dataframe with species as ROWS
  as.data.frame(t(transect_mat)),
  #dist object above
  dist_dbfd,
  #the default for scale is F, but since it is undocumented better be explicit
  scale = F)

Unsurprisingly, the two give the same result, but it is not the same as raoq(). Why?

all.equal(unname(rao_dbfd), rao_ade4$diversity)

[1] TRUE

all.equal(rao_ade4$diversity, transect_nested$Rao)

[1] "Mean relative difference: 2.134283"


Inspecting the source, divc() does the same cross product trick, but column by column so it’s less efficient. Then, despite referencing Rao (1982), it performs a slightly different calculation: the distance matrix is squared, and the column result is divided by two and divided again by the squared sum of abundances. Putting aside the squared sum thing (that part is just scaling the raw abundances/presences/frequencies into proportions after the fact), this is actually the “Euclidean diversity coefficient” of Champely and Chessel (2002)! The reasoning behind it is that if distance used is the Euclidean distance, this equals the variance of the trait distribution see Appendix C of my article. This has been observed by Bello et al. (2016) too.
The scaling part is not an issue, the documentation does say “abundance, presence-absence or frequencies as entries”, and if you feed proportions it’s harmless, but divc() does the distance transformation behind the scenes, only checking if the distance matrix is Euclidean, even if it’s not the Euclidean. If we take the guts of divc, remove some input checks, and change one line to remove the \(\Delta = \frac{d^{2}}{2}\) part to go back to the original Rao formula, we get something like this:

fakedivc <- function (df, dis = NULL, scale = FALSE) 
{
  div <- as.data.frame(rep(0, ncol(df)))
  names(div) <- "diversity"
  rownames(div) <- names(df)
  for (i in 1:ncol(df)) {
    if (sum(df[, i]) < 1e-16) 
      div[i, ] <- 0
    else div[i, ] <- (t(df[, i]) %*% (as.matrix(dis)) %*% df[, i])/(sum(df[, i])^2)
  }
  if (scale == TRUE) {
    divmax <- divcmax(dis)$value
    div <- div/divmax
  }
  return(div)
}

And, sure enough, things match now.

rao_ade4_fake <- fakedivc(as.data.frame(t(transect_mat)),
                          dist_dbfd,
                          scale = F)

all.equal(rao_ade4_fake$diversity, transect_nested$Rao)

[1] TRUE


adiv::QE() is basically the same as these two, down to the source code, but it does have the option to choose between quadratic entropy and Euclidean diversity index:

rao_adiv <- adiv::QE(transect_mat,
                     dist_dbfd,
                     "QE") |> 
  pull()

all.equal(rao_adiv, transect_nested$Rao)

[1] TRUE

text:
fundiversity
I agree, diversity is fun. This package seems cool, and the function fd_raoq() too. It can accept either traits or distances, has a nice helper to subset it and the community if the species don’t match, and uses the cross product under the hood. The results are the same as with raoq():

rao_fun <- fundiversity::fd_raoq(sp_com = transect_mat,
                                 dist_matrix = distances) |> 
  pluck("Q")
  
all.equal(rao_fun, transect_nested$Rao)

[1] TRUE

title: Calculating Rao with R
text:
mFD
This function is one of those that calculates generalizations of functional diversity. Being based on Hill numbers, what it returns is actually the equivalent number \(E = \frac{1}{1-Q}\) but you only notice this if you pay attention to the cited literature and to the phrase “is equivalent to”, which doesn’t mean “equals”. Once we retransform the values, things add up.






Caution



While this function supports both matrices and dist objects, I got different results using dist_dbfd from above. The reason is that the distance matrix is automatically scaled, whether you want it or not, and dist_dbfd is a subset of the full matrix. This is something to keep in mind, especially if you try to compare samples calculated with different distance matrices.



rao_mfd <- mFD::alpha.fd.hill(transect_mat,
                              distances,
                              q = 2,
                              tau = "max",
                              details_returned = F)

rao_mfd <- 1 - 1 / rao_mfd[, 1]

all.equal(unname(rao_mfd), transect_nested$Rao)

[1] TRUE

title: Calculating Rao with R
text:
hillR
Another function that calculates Hill number generalizations of functional diversity. We can calculate Rao by setting q = 2. In theory, you can provide either traits, or a “symmetric distance matrix” with traits_as_is: this is a lie, it wants a dist instead. Works fine otherwise. Unlike mFD(), it provides both Rao and functional Hill numbers, so you can pick your favourite.

rao_hillr <- hillR::hill_func(transect_mat, dist_dbfd, traits_as_is = T, q = 2, fdis = F)["Q", ]

all.equal(unname(rao_hillr), transect_nested$Rao)

[1] TRUE

title: Calculating Rao with R
Calculating Rao with R
text:
Performance comparison
The authors of fundiversity seem to care about performance, since they did an overview of available packages and benchmarked them together. One thing I noticed about fd_raoq() is that it calculates Rao even with pairs of abundance vectors from different communities. That could be useful as a first step to calculate the original Rao dissimilarity, but here they are just discarded. How will it perform against the others?

dist_subset <- as.matrix(dist_dbfd)

#suppressMessages is so that FD would shut up
bench <- bench::mark(
  raoq_map = map_dbl(transect_nested$data, \(x) raoq(x$prop, distances, x$species)),
  raoq_mat = apply(transect_mat, 1, function(x) raoq(x, dist_subset)),
  FD = FD::dbFD(x = dist_dbfd,
           a = transect_mat,
           w.abun = T,
           calc.FRic = F,
           calc.FDiv = F,
           calc.CWM = F,
           messages = F),
  ade4 = ade4::divc(as.data.frame(t(transect_mat)),
             dist_dbfd,
             scale = F),
  adiv = adiv::QE(transect_mat, dist_dbfd, "QE"),
  fundiversity = fundiversity::fd_raoq(sp_com = transect_mat, dist_matrix = distances),
  mFD = mFD::alpha.fd.hill(transect_mat, distances, q = 2, tau = "max", details_returned = F),
  hillR = hillR::hill_func(transect_mat, dist_dbfd, traits_as_is = T, q = 2, fdis = F),
  melodic = melodic(transect_mat, distances, "abundance"),
  check = F) |> 
  arrange(median)

fd_raoq() still wins, with raoq() close behind! This is the power of primitve matrix operations: even when computing N2 indices instead of N, this is still faster if you can do it with matrix products instead of row by row. This holds true even when the distance matrix is subset beforehand, instead of each iteration (raoq_map).
Learning from this and taking up the challenge, can we make raoq() fast? Since the trick is to use only matrix operations, we turn to the community matrix, instead of iterating over single vectors of proportions. This has the advantage that we don’t need to have a separate species argument, we can just use column names as everyone else. Turns out we don’t need to do the big N2 cross product, we can do something similar to what I did when explaining the double cross product by just doing multiplication followed by summing columns. We can have our cake and eat it too, or as they say in Italy, you can have a full cask and a drunk wife (I’m not a fan of cake, wine, or sexist sayings either):

raoq_fast <- function(com, dist){
  #subset species in the distance matrix if necessary
  species <- colnames(com)
  dist <- dist[species, species]
  #it's called rowSums because it sums together columns by row
  rowSums((com %*% dist) * com)
}

rao_raoqfast <- raoq_fast(transect_mat, distances)

all.equal(unname(rao_raoqfast), rao_fun)

[1] TRUE

rebench <- bench::mark(
  raoq_fast = unname(raoq_fast(transect_mat, distances)),
  fd_raoq = fundiversity::fd_raoq(sp_com = transect_mat, dist_matrix = distances),
  check = F) |> 
  arrange(median)

rebench

# A tibble: 2 × 6
  expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
  <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
1 raoq_fast      41µs  44.91µs    19487.  113.94KB     47.0
2 fd_raoq       1.2ms   1.27ms      620.    2.68MB     53.2


Well well! About 40 to 50 times faster than fd_raoq()!

title: Calculating Rao with R
text:
Conclusions
In practice, the speed differences are irrelevant, except maybe for dbFD(because it calculates a bunch of other things). Since FD, ade4 and adiv calculate their own version of Rao, I would use either my functions, adiv, fundiversity, or melodic. If you’re into Hill numbers, the mFD and hillR packages are interesting, but you can always transform Rao yourself if you stick with q = 2. Between my two functions, I would probably still use the slower one, because iterating explicitly gives me more control over the output format. Another thing of note is whether the functions require you to subset the distance matrix beforehand or they take care of it themselves, and whether they want a matrix or a dist. I consider functions that can take a matrix and can subset or rearrange it more robust, and those would be raoq()(either one), fd_raoq(), alpha.fd.hill(), and melodic().
I hope this is useful to someone. The first thought when having to calculate an index might be “oh, I’ll just grab a package that does it”, but we have seen how things are not as simple as that in this case. This is not meant to be a comprehensive overview, but to include many popular solutions as well as providing some interesting alternatives.

title: Calculating Rao with R
text:
Extra: decomposition
I mentioned at the beginning that the \(\alpha\) formula is just a small part of what you can do, and you can go further with a nested decomposition in the style of \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\).
To give you a taste of that, I’ll share a function I made for De Benedictis et al. (2026) which calculates a bunch of Rao-based indices. Compared to the original, I changed the input format to the classical community matrix, raoq() with the updated version with name matching (instead of factors, ugh), and the internal data format to the convention “species on columns, samples on rows”. The indices are described in De Bello et al. (2010) and Pavoine and Ricotta (2024).

qdecomp <- function(data, distances){
  #alpha Q
  alpha <- apply(data, 1, function(x) raoq(x, distances, names(x))) |>
    mean()
  #regional relative abundances as mean of local ab.
  #this gives equal weight to each community
  P_i <- colMeans(data)
  #gamma Q
  gamma <- raoq(P_i, distances, names(P_i))
  #additive beta
  beta_add <- gamma - alpha
  #additive beta normalized by gamma
  beta_rel <- beta_add / gamma
  #equivalent alpha
  E_alpha <- 1/(1-alpha)
  #equivalent gamma
  E_gamma <- 1/(1-gamma)
  #multiplicative eq. beta
  E_beta_mult <- E_gamma / E_alpha
  #additive eq. beta
  E_beta_add <- E_gamma - E_alpha
  #proportional additive beta, normalized on sample n
  E_beta_add_prop_norm <- (E_beta_add / E_gamma) / (1 - 1 / nrow(data))
  #matrix of taxonomic distances (0/1)
  taxon <- distances
  taxon[,] <- 1
  diag(taxon) <- 0
  #taxonomic alpha
  alpha_sp <- apply(data, 1, function(x) raoq(x, taxon, names(x))) |> 
    mean()
  #taxonomic gamma
  gamma_sp <- raoq(P_i, taxon, names(P_i))
  #additive tax. beta
  beta_sp_add <- gamma_sp - alpha_sp
  #normalized tax. beta
  beta_sp_rel <- beta_sp_add / gamma_sp
  #equivalent tax. alpha
  E_alpha_sp <- 1/(1-alpha_sp)
  #equivalent tax. gamma
  E_gamma_sp <- 1/(1-gamma_sp)
  #equivalent tax. beta
  E_beta_sp <- E_gamma_sp / E_alpha_sp
  #beta Q clustering
  clustering <- beta_rel / beta_sp_rel
  #gamma Q uniqueness
  uniqueness <- gamma / gamma_sp
  #gamma E uniqueness
  U_gamma_star <- E_gamma / E_gamma_sp
  #alpha E redundancy, inverse of Ualpha_star
  redundancy_a <- E_alpha_sp / E_alpha
  
  output <- data.frame(alpha, gamma, beta_add, beta_rel,
                       E_alpha, E_gamma, E_beta_mult, E_beta_add,
                       E_beta_add_prop_norm, clustering, uniqueness,
                       alpha_sp, gamma_sp, U_gamma_star, redundancy_a,
                       beta_sp_add, E_alpha_sp, E_gamma_sp, E_beta_sp)
  return(output)
}

title: Fitting the gravitational constant with brms
text: My experience with astronomy and astrophysics boils down to teenage curiosity. The main purpose of this example is as an exercise in brms nonlinear syntax. There are probably many tiny errors and things that could be done better. The way the variables are used doesn’t have to reflect the order in which they were inferred, it’s purely a statistical exercise. A more realistic story would be to weigh things on Earth and then use the inferred gravitational constant to find out the mass of astronomical bodies.

title: Fitting the gravitational constant with brms
text:
What?
In some disciplines, there is a disconnect between scientific theory and use of models and current practice. In physics, for example, theory often results in an explicit functional form, this model is tested against reality, and it is provisionally kept as long as there are no obvious discrepancies with observation. If and when those arise, it’s an incentive to question the model and look for a better one. In many other scientific fields, the role of falsification seems like the opposite: nobody really believes the “null” model represents reality, and observing a lack of fit to data is the goal. Null hypothesis rejected, you discovered something new (maybe) and you win! This contrast has been highlighted several times, for example by Meehl (1967).
It doesn’t have to be like this. Even when fitting statistical models to empirical data, sometimes you’re lucky and theory provides you with a formula that you can use in place of an additive linear model. Chapter 16 of McElreath (2020) is dedicated to examples of this, including one with the Lotka-Volterra equations. Nonlinear model formulas are key to this approach, so, with the purpose of getting in some exercise with them in brms, I have developed the following contrived example:
Let’s fit Kepler’s third law in brms to find the gravitational constant G
What I mean exactly is the formula that you get by substituting Newton’s law of gravitation into Kepler’s law
\[\frac{a^{3}}{T^{2}}=\frac{G(M+m)}{4\pi^{2}}\]
What data to fit this to? I found a website that lets you freely download data about solar system bodies in a machine-readable way. For simplicity, I’m restricting this to moons orbiting around planets, since the two are easy to combine in their data format.

title: Fitting the gravitational constant with brms
text:
Setup

library(conflicted)
library(tidyverse)
library(httr)
library(brms)
library(ggdist)

conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter,
                 brms::ar,
                 brms::dstudent_t,
                 brms::pstudent_t,
                 brms::qstudent_t,
                 brms::rstudent_t,
                 stats::lag)

#please use cmdstanr, it's so much faster
options(cores = parallel::detectCores(),
        brms.backend = "cmdstanr",
        pillar.sigfig = 6)

theme_set(theme_minimal())

title: Fitting the gravitational constant with brms
text:
Get the data

#this is my key, stored locally. You can get your own, it's free
key <- read_lines("apikey.txt")

#moon data
moons <- GET("https://api.le-systeme-solaire.net/rest/bodies/", 
           add_headers(Authorization = paste("Bearer", key)),
           query = list(`filter[]` = "bodyType,eq,Moon")) |> 
  content()

#planet data
planets <- GET("https://api.le-systeme-solaire.net/rest/bodies/", 
               add_headers(Authorization = paste("Bearer", key)),
               query = list(`filter[]` = "bodyType,eq,Planet")) |> 
  content()

useful <- c("id", "englishName", "semimajorAxis", "mass", "sideralOrbit", "aroundPlanet")

#wrangle this ugly list into a nice tibble
planets <- planets$bodies |> 
  map(\(x) x |> 
        #some elements are null, some are lists of length 2
        #as_tibble_row complains, that's why the gymnastics
        discard(is_null) |> 
        enframe() |> 
        pivot_wider()) |> 
  #bind the planet rows into a tibble
  bind_rows() |> 
  #keep only what's necessary
  select(any_of(useful)) |> 
  #mass is in scientific notation across two fields
  mutate(mass = map_dbl(mass, \(x) x$massValue * 10^x$massExponent)) |>
  #undo the list-cols created by enframe() |> pivot_wider()
  mutate(across(everything(), unlist))

title: Fitting the gravitational constant with brms
text:
Fit the model
Since the data is literally on astronomical scales, I thought it wise to fit the model on a log10-transformed version of the equation. While this might take some of the nonlinear charm away, since a big product is transformed in a more familiar sum, we will see that the nonlinear formula will still let us specify the model in a way that would just break with a traditional model formula.
The parameter to fit is G, but we still need some meaningful outcome on the LHS. I decided to solve for \(\widehat{M} = M +m\)
\[\widehat{M}=\frac{4\pi^{2}a^{3}}{T^2G}\]
Then, taking the log10 of both sides
\[\log M = -\log G+\log4\pi^2+3\log a-2\log T\]
This translates directly into the nonlinear formula. Unlike the usual model formulas, regression coefficients (what you multiply the sum terms with) are explicit, so any parameter must be specified with a unique name in the formula. This lets us say explicitly that the last two terms must be multiplied by 3 and 2, not with parameters estimated from the data. The parameter to estimate, logG, has its own intercept-only model.

formula <- bf(log10(M) ~ -logG + log10(4*pi^2) + 3*log10(a) - 2*log10(T),
              logG ~ 1,
              nl = T)

Since I’m not an astronomer, I’ll pretend I have no domain knowledge outside “planets are big, and moons as well” and use default priors just this once. The model fits fine in case you’re worried.

text:
Generate predictions
While this is a fine demonstration of nonlinear brms models, at the beginning I mentioned facing the model with reality. To do this we can take the estimated value of G (with all its posterior distribution) and generate predictions on a separate dataset. In this case, I’ll predict the orbital period of planets around the sun using G, masses, and semi-major axes.
\[T = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi^{2}a^{3}}{G\widehat{M}}}\]

  arrange(sideralOrbit) |> 
  mutate(
    englishName = fct(englishName),
    #the mass of the sun in kg
    mass_sun = 1.988475e30,
    M = mass + mass_sun,
    #convert semi-major axis to meters
    a = semimajorAxis * 1000,
    #convert sideral orbit to seconds
    T = sideralOrbit * 24 * 3600,
    #remind the value of pi to the model
    pi = pi)

title: Starting a blog!
text:
Scientific debate currently revolves around papers, being the agreed upon way to make science, but they can’t be the only outlet for scholarly discussion. Post-publication review is still mostly theory, and post-publication is often severely lacking. Response articles exist, but usually you don’t want to go through months of peer review unless it’s something really big, and it seems more of a way to get into an academic fight than anything at times.
So, what do we have? Conferences are one option, but they involve a restricted number of people at one specific time. Mostly, the discussion of published material involves some off-handed comments while referencing it, lost in the body of a text. And then there’s the blog, this old-fashioned way to use the internet.
I’m not ashamed to say that I have learnt more from some posts on blogs such as those in resources than from some papers. Inspired by those and others, I decided to start a blog, in the hope of doing a bit of the same myself. Posts could be small ideas, or just practical examples. Some of the latter come from my own work, where they might have been small technicalities, shadowed by the bigger goal and message, which could be of broader interest despite their simplicity.
I have focused a lot on discussion, and surely there is the possibility of real-time discussion, as allowed by the internet, but I also intend this in the broader terms: publishing something for people to read and benefit from is already part of a discussion. So, I’m happy to write about what I like to do in a less formal way, and you’re welcome to just read the incoming posts, maybe benefit from them or even acknowledge the help!
Have a nice stay here.

title: Tidy ecology with R
text:
Note



This post and its twin were conceived together. In my mind, the two topics are tightly linked, but a tangent about different software implementations of a diversity index grew so large that it deserved its own post. If you’re interested in both, you can read that one after this.
There is a tradition in ecology to represent community data in a “community matrix” (Legendre and Legendre 2012). This what we can call a “wide” format, with species on columns and samples on rows. I prefer this convention to having them the other way around, since we can treat species as “variables” and samples as “observations”.
The popular package vegan interprets this literally as matrix objects. Matrices in R have nice uses, for example if you want to exploit matrix algebra for the fastest calculations, but they are raw and ugly to print and view, definitely not what you would want for general data analysis. The package tidyvegan seems to share this sentiment, adapting the most useful functions in the package to the use of tibbles and the pipe-friendly “data as first argument” convention.
The thing is, community data is often awfully sparse. Wouldn’t it be nice to work in a long format? That has often been my preference, so I’ll show you how to reconcile the two worlds without too much pain. Spoiler: this mostly involves the use of pivot_wider() and pivot_longer(), but I think the practical examples and some added details make this worth sharing.

This gets especially confusing when you try to do normal matrix operations like subsetting, since the underlying object is one-dimensional:

try(plain2[1, 1])

Error in plain2[1, 1] : incorrect number of dimensions


I think it’s best to call as.matrix() right away and work with the full symmetrical matrix, then handle it as needed.
Finally, maybe I would like to let stats and vegan enjoy their matrices and look at the output in a tibble instead. Let’s say we want to use those distance values as data in a model, as we did in the paper above. To do all this behind the scenes, I made two helper functions, which I have now adapted for more general use:

vegan_cook <- function(x, species_col = "species", value_col = "cover", sample_name = NULL){
  
  if(is.null(sample_name)) sample_name <- setdiff(names(x), c(species_col, value_col))
  if(length(sample_name) > 1) stop("Please provide a unique identifier column for samples")
  
  x |> 
    pivot_wider(names_from = all_of(species_col), values_from = all_of(value_col), values_fill = 0) |> 
    column_to_rownames(sample_name) |> 
    as.matrix()
}

tidyvegdist <- function(x, sample_names = "sample", diag = F, tri = F, ...){
  
  if(length(sample_names) == 1) sample_names <- str_c(sample_names, 1:2, sep = "_")
  
  vegdist(x, ...) |> 
    as.matrix() |> 
    (\(m) {if (tri) m[upper.tri(m, diag = F)] <- NA; m})() |> 
    (\(m) {if (!diag) diag(m) <- NA; m})() |> 
    as_tibble(rownames = sample_names[1]) |> 
    pivot_longer(!all_of(sample_names[1]), names_to = sample_names[2]) |> 
    drop_na()
}

vegan_cook() handles the forward transformation into a vegan matrix. You can specify the names of the columns to pivot from with species_col and value_col. The row (sample) name columns is gathered automatically from the remaining column, or can be specified manually. tidyvegdist() calls vegdist() and returns a long tibble. You can choose how to call the columns with the pair names, either with an atomic string, which gets suffixes, or with a character vector. It defaults to "sample"; you can choose to include the diagonal values (usually 0) with diag, or to get a triangular matrix instead of the full symmetric matrix with tri; finally, you can pass other arguments to vegdist(), such as method.

Example 2: transect data
The second example is a snippet from the data of De Benedictis et al. (2026). This is a peculiar case, because it comes from a 1000-unit looping transect which has been resampled with overlap at several scales, so there are many sampling units, but each has few records because they come from beech forest understory. This is just one scale of one transect. For each sampling unit X, row represent observations of a species. When the sampling units are aggregates as in this case, these can be used to calculate frequencies.
